lead: Moist air is a mixture of dry air and water vapour. Its state decides whether a room feels comfortable, whether clothes dry on a line, and how much water a cooling tower evaporates. Psychrometry gives four linked measures: dry-bulb temperature, humidity ratio, relative humidity and dew point. The psychrometric chart plots them together so heating, cooling and drying paths can be read without solving equations each time.
prereq: You need 5.9 Dalton's law for partial pressures and 5.5 steam tables for psat(T).

sections.h3: Dry air, vapour and humidity ratio

blocks.text: Moist air is dry air plus water vapour. At ordinary pressures both behave as ideal gases, so Dalton's law applies: the total pressure p is the sum of the dry-air partial pressure p<sub>a</sub> and the vapour partial pressure p<sub>v</sub>. The dry-bulb temperature T is the temperature read by an ordinary thermometer in the air, with no water on its bulb.

blocks.where: φ is relative humidity, from 0 to 1; p<sub>v</sub> is the water-vapour partial pressure in kPa; p<sub>sat</sub>(T) is the saturation pressure of water at the dry-bulb temperature T, read from steam tables.

blocks.text: Relative humidity is a ratio of pressures, not a ratio of masses. It says how close the vapour is to condensing. φ = 1 means saturated air.

blocks.where: w is the humidity ratio in kg water vapour per kg dry air; 0.622 = 18.015/28.97 is the molar mass ratio; p is total pressure in kPa; p<sub>v</sub> is vapour partial pressure in kPa.

blocks.text: Here p − p<sub>v</sub> is p<sub>a</sub>, the dry-air pressure. The factor 0.622 comes from the molar masses: 18.015 g/mol for water and 28.97 g/mol for dry air. Using total p in the denominator instead of p<sub>a</sub> is a common error.

blocks.where: h is the enthalpy of moist air in kJ per kg dry air; T is dry-bulb temperature in °C; 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) is the specific heat of dry air; 2500 kJ/kg is the latent heat of water at 0 °C; 1.86 kJ/(kg·K) is the specific heat of water vapour.

blocks.text: The enthalpy of moist air is quoted per kg of dry air. The first term is the dry-air enthalpy; the bracket is the vapour enthalpy. This approximation is accurate enough for comfort air-conditioning.

Two more measures appear in exam questions. The degree of saturation μ = w/w<sub>s</sub> compares w with the humidity ratio of saturated air at the same temperature; it is close to φ but not equal. The specific volume of moist air, per kg of dry air, is v = R<sub>a</sub>T/p<sub>a</sub> with R<sub>a</sub> = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) and T in kelvin.

The dew point T<sub>dp</sub> is the temperature at which the vapour just becomes saturated at the same p<sub>v</sub>. It satisfies p<sub>sat</sub>(T<sub>dp</sub>) = p<sub>v</sub>. If moist air is cooled at constant pressure and constant w, the first change is a fall in T; the dew point is reached when the relative humidity becomes 100%. Further cooling makes liquid water condense. This is why a cold water bottle sweats in a Chennai room.

The wet-bulb temperature T<sub>wb</sub> is read by a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet cloth and exposed to moving air. Water evaporates from the cloth and cools the bulb. The drier the air, the faster the evaporation and the lower the wet-bulb reading. For unsaturated air, T<sub>dp</sub> < T<sub>wb</sub> < T<sub>db</sub>. At saturation all three are equal.

Wet-bulb and dew point answer different questions. Dew point is reached by cooling without evaporation. Wet-bulb is reached by evaporating water into the air and cooling it. For air-water vapour the wet-bulb temperature is close to the adiabatic saturation temperature, which is why the chart uses one line family for both.

The chart plots humidity ratio w on the vertical axis against dry-bulb temperature T on the horizontal axis, at one fixed total pressure, usually 101.325 kPa. The curved saturation line is φ = 100%. Above it is fog or condensation; below it is unsaturated moist air.

Constant relative humidity lines curve down from the saturation line; the 60% line lies below the 100% line. Constant enthalpy and constant wet-bulb lines run nearly parallel, sloping down to the right. The state point fixes all properties: read w on the vertical scale and T on the horizontal scale.

Sensible heating moves the state point horizontally to the right: w stays fixed, T rises, and φ falls. Cooling moves it horizontally left; when the saturation line is reached, further cooling follows the curve and water condenses out. Adding water vapour moves the point upward: with a fine water spray the air also cools slightly as the water evaporates, while adding steam raises the temperature. The chart turns these paths into straight-line steps, which is why it survives in air-conditioning work.

examples.question: Moist air at 30 °C dry-bulb and 60% relative humidity flows at a total pressure of 101.325 kPa. The saturation pressure of water is 4.247 kPa at 30 °C, 2.488 kPa at 21 °C and 2.645 kPa at 22 °C. Find the vapour partial pressure, the humidity ratio, the degree of saturation, the dew point, the enthalpy and the specific volume per kg of dry air.
steps: Vapour partial pressure: p<sub>v</sub> = φ × p<sub>sat</sub>(30 °C) = 0.60 × 4.247 = 2.548 kPa.
Dry-air partial pressure: p<sub>a</sub> = p − p<sub>v</sub> = 101.325 − 2.548 = 98.777 kPa.
Humidity ratio: w = 0.622 × 2.548/98.777 = 0.01605 kg/kg dry air.
Dew point: p<sub>sat</sub>(T<sub>dp</sub>) = 2.548 kPa lies between 21 °C and 22 °C: T<sub>dp</sub> = 21 + (2.548 − 2.488)/(2.645 − 2.488) = 21 + 0.060/0.157 = 21.4 °C.
Specific volume: v = R<sub>a</sub>T/p<sub>a</sub> = 0.287 × 303.15/98.777 = 0.881 m³/kg dry air.
examples.answer: p<sub>v</sub> = 2.548 kPa, w = 0.0160 kg/kg dry air, μ = 0.590, T<sub>dp</sub> ≈ 21.4 °C, h ≈ 71.2 kJ/kg dry air and v ≈ 0.881 m³/kg dry air.

traps: Using total pressure p instead of dry-air pressure p − p<sub>v</sub> in the humidity-ratio formula. The error is small at low humidity but large near saturation.
Treating relative humidity as a mass ratio. φ compares p<sub>v</sub> with p<sub>sat</sub> at the same dry-bulb temperature.
Taking the wet-bulb temperature as the dew point. They coincide only at saturation.
Using p<sub>sat</sub> at the wet-bulb or dew-point temperature when the question gives φ at the dry-bulb temperature. Use p<sub>sat</sub>(T<sub>db</sub>).
Forgetting that humidity ratio is per kg of dry air, not per kg of moist air.

quiz.q: Define dry-bulb temperature and dew point in one line each.
quiz.a: Dry-bulb temperature is the temperature read by an ordinary thermometer in the air. Dew point is the temperature at which the vapour in the air just becomes saturated at the same vapour partial pressure.

quiz.q: Write the humidity-ratio formula for air-water vapour and state what 0.622 represents.
quiz.a: w = 0.622 p<sub>v</sub> / (p − p<sub>v</sub>). The number 0.622 is the ratio of the molar mass of water, 18.015 g/mol, to the molar mass of dry air, 28.97 g/mol.

quiz.q: For unsaturated moist air, why is the dew point lower than the wet-bulb temperature, and the wet-bulb lower than the dry-bulb?
quiz.a: Dew point is reached by cooling the air until p<sub>v</sub> equals p<sub>sat</sub>; no evaporation is involved. Wet-bulb is reached when evaporation from a wet wick cools the bulb; evaporation stops only when the air near the wick is saturated, so T<sub>wb</sub> is above T<sub>dp</sub>. Dry-bulb is the true air temperature, and evaporative cooling lowers the bulb below it, so T<sub>dp</sub> < T<sub>wb</sub> < T<sub>db</sub>.

quiz.q: Moist air at 25 °C dry-bulb and 50% relative humidity is at 101.325 kPa. Saturation pressure at 25 °C is 3.169 kPa. Find p<sub>v</sub> and w.
At 30 °C dry-bulb, p<sub>v</sub> = 2.548 kPa and total pressure is 101.325 kPa. Saturation pressure at 30 °C is 4.247 kPa. Find φ and w.
On a psychrometric chart, a cooling process starts at 30 °C and w = 0.016 kg/kg dry air and moves left at constant w. Describe the path and what happens after the saturation line is reached.
quiz.a: At constant w the state moves horizontally left, so dry-bulb temperature falls while humidity ratio stays fixed. Relative humidity rises. When the saturation curve is reached, the air is saturated and the temperature there is the dew point, about 21.4 °C. Further cooling follows the saturation curve; water condenses out and w decreases along the curve.

quiz.q: A room is at 30 °C and 60% relative humidity. A glass of water at 15 °C is placed in it. Saturation pressure at 15 °C is 1.705 kPa and at 30 °C is 4.247 kPa. Will moisture condense on the glass? Give the reason.
quiz.a: p<sub>v</sub> in the room is 0.60 × 4.247 = 2.548 kPa, so the dew point is about 21.4 °C. The glass surface is at 15 °C, where p<sub>sat</sub> = 1.705 kPa. The air touching the glass is cooled below its dew point (p<sub>v</sub> = 2.548 kPa is more than 1.705 kPa), so water condenses on the glass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Psychrometry drives air-conditioning load calculations, cooling-tower design, grain and fruit drying, and weather forecasting. Modern software uses the same equations you met here but adds real-gas corrections near saturation. Search for psychrometric chart, wet-bulb temperature and sling psychrometer to go further.
